title: Jeremiah 48:29–47
context: The LORD names Moab’s pride and then speaks of wailing and weeping for Moab, with images of a ruined vineyard, silenced wine presses, and mourning customs. The tone mixes judgment with grief. Several lines closely resemble Isaiah 15-16, and 48:43-44 resembles Isaiah 24:17-18, while 48:45-46 echoes the ancient song of Numbers 21:28-29. The chapter closes with a promise that the LORD will reverse the captivity of Moab in the latter days, a note of mercy shared by both traditions, similar to promises for Egypt, Ammon, and Elam (46:26; 49:6; 49:39).

verses.text: “We have heard of the pride of Moab. He is very proud in his loftiness, his pride, his arrogance, and the arrogance of his heart.
verses.arminianNotes: We have heard of the pride of Moab. Arminian readers see pride named as Moab’s central sin, listed again and again in loftiness, pride, arrogance, and the arrogance of his heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Isaiah 16:6 opens with the same words and also lists Moab’s arrogance and pride. The repetition of words for pride stresses the depth of the problem.

verses.text: I know his wrath,” says the LORD, “that it is nothing; his boastings have done nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: I know his wrath, Arminian readers see the LORD weighing Moab’s fury and finding that it is nothing, its boastings achieving nothing in the end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Isaiah 16:6 likewise says that Moab’s boastings are nothing. The LORD’s knowledge of Moab’s heart contrasts with Moab’s inflated estimate of itself.

verses.text: Therefore I will wail for Moab. Yes, I will cry out for all Moab. They will mourn for the men of Kir Heres.
verses.arminianNotes: Therefore I will wail for Moab. Arminian readers see deep compassion even in judgment; the speaker grieves for Moab and for the men of Kir Heres rather than rejoicing at their fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the voice may be the prophet’s or the LORD’s, and readers differ. The Isaiah 15:5 and Isaiah 16:9 boxes treat this kind of grief over Moab; compare Isaiah 16:7 for Kir Hareseth.

verses.text: With more than the weeping of Jazer I will weep for you, vine of Sibmah. Your branches passed over the sea. They reached even to the sea of Jazer. The destroyer has fallen on your summer fruits and on your vintage.
verses.arminianNotes: With more than the weeping of Jazer I will weep for you, vine of Sibmah. Arminian readers see grief poured out over Moab’s vineyards, its spreading branches now struck by the destroyer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers find Isaiah 16:8-9 very similar, which also speaks of Jazer, the vine of Sibmah, and branches that passed over the sea. The locations are uncertain.

verses.text: Gladness and joy is taken away from the fruitful field and from the land of Moab. I have caused wine to cease from the wine presses. No one will tread with shouting. The shouting will be no shouting.
verses.arminianNotes: Gladness and joy is taken away from the fruitful field and from the land of Moab. Arminian readers see the end of the harvest celebrations that marked Moab’s seasons of plenty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD says, I have caused wine to cease from the wine presses, wording close to Isaiah 16:10. The shouting of joy gives way to silence.

verses.text: From the cry of Heshbon even to Elealeh, even to Jahaz they have uttered their voice, from Zoar even to Horonaim, to Eglath Shelishiyah; for the waters of Nimrim will also become desolate.
verses.arminianNotes: From the cry of Heshbon even to Elealeh, even to Jahaz they have uttered their voice, Arminian readers see a cry spreading across the land from town to town as the disaster unfolds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the place names closely resemble Isaiah 15:4-6, including Zoar, Eglath Shelishiyah, and the waters of Nimrim. The sites are identified only tentatively.

verses.text: Moreover I will cause to cease in Moab,” says the LORD, “him who offers in the high place, and him who burns incense to his gods.
verses.arminianNotes: Moreover I will cause to cease in Moab, Arminian readers see the LORD halting Moab’s offerings at the high place and its incense to its gods, showing the emptiness of idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers point out that Isaiah 16:12 also speaks of Moab praying at its high place without prevailing. The LORD brings false worship to an end along with the nation’s prosperity.

verses.text: Therefore my heart sounds for Moab like flutes, and my heart sounds like flutes for the men of Kir Heres. Therefore the abundance that he has gotten has perished.
verses.arminianNotes: Therefore my heart sounds for Moab like flutes, Arminian readers see grief expressed through music, the speaker’s heart sounding a mournful note over the fall of Moab’s cities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Isaiah 16:11, which uses a harp rather than flutes; the Isaiah 16:11 box treats this image. The abundance that Moab had gotten has perished, compare Isaiah 15:7.

verses.text: For every head is bald, and every beard clipped. There are cuttings on all the hands, and sackcloth on the waist.
verses.arminianNotes: For every head is bald, and every beard clipped. Arminian readers recognize mourning customs of the ancient world, signs of grief worn openly across the land, described here without excess.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the cuttings on the hands and sackcloth on the waist are signs of mourning also named in Isaiah 15:2-3. The verse pictures a whole people in grief.

verses.text: On all the housetops of Moab, and in its streets, there is lamentation everywhere; for I have broken Moab like a vessel in which no one delights,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: On all the housetops of Moab, and in its streets, there is lamentation everywhere; Arminian readers see grief filling homes and streets, a land overwhelmed by sorrow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the LORD’s words, I have broken Moab like a vessel in which no one delights. The image recalls Jeremiah’s breaking of the flask in 19:10-11.

verses.text: “How it is broken down! How they wail! How Moab has turned the back with shame! So will Moab become a derision and a terror to all who are around him.”
verses.arminianNotes: How it is broken down! How they wail! Arminian readers hear the lament turning to the shame of Moab, which has turned the back and become a derision to its neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Moab becomes a derision and a terror to all who are around him. The one who mocked Israel in 48:27 now suffers the same contempt.

verses.text: For the LORD says: “Behold, he will fly as an eagle, and will spread out his wings against Moab.
verses.arminianNotes: For the LORD says: Arminian readers see the image of an eagle spreading its wings against Moab, a swift and overwhelming enemy whose identity the verse does not name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the eagle is often taken to be Babylon, though that is an inference. Jeremiah 49:22 uses the same image against Edom; see the Judges 9:23 box on God using hostile agents.

verses.text: Kerioth is taken, and the strongholds are seized. The heart of the mighty men of Moab at that day will be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.
verses.arminianNotes: Kerioth is taken, and the strongholds are seized. Arminian readers see the courage of Moab’s warriors failing, their hearts like a woman in her pangs, an image of helpless anguish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah 49:22 applies nearly the same words to Edom. The prophets often use the image of labor pains for terror before judgment.

verses.text: Moab will be destroyed from being a people, because he has magnified himself against the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Moab will be destroyed from being a people, because he has magnified himself against the LORD. Arminian readers see the reason restated: pride against God leads to the loss of national life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the charge repeats 48:26. Both traditions read the verse as judgment on a nation’s pride, without drawing conclusions about the eternal state of individuals.

verses.text: Terror, the pit, and the snare are on you, inhabitant of Moab,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Terror, the pit, and the snare are on you, inhabitant of Moab, Arminian readers observe how closely this resembles Isaiah 24:17, where similar words are spoken to the inhabitants of the earth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image of inescapable judgment: three dangers set one after another. The wording that Isaiah applies to the whole earth is applied here to Moab specifically.

verses.text: “He who flees from the terror will fall into the pit; and he who gets up out of the pit will be taken in the snare, for I will bring on him, even on Moab, the year of their visitation,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: He who flees from the terror will fall into the pit; Arminian readers see each attempt to escape leading into another trap, a picture of judgment that cannot be outrun.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Isaiah 24:18 has nearly the same sequence of pit and snare. The verse ends with the year of their visitation, a time appointed by the LORD.

verses.text: “Those who fled stand without strength under the shadow of Heshbon; for a fire has gone out of Heshbon, and a flame from the middle of Sihon, and has devoured the corner of Moab, and the crown of the head of the tumultuous ones.
verses.arminianNotes: Those who fled stand without strength under the shadow of Heshbon; Arminian readers see refugees finding no shelter, as fire goes out from Heshbon and from the middle of Sihon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the lines echo Numbers 21:28, an old song about a fire from Heshbon, the city of Sihon. The phrase the corner of Moab may also recall Numbers 24:17, though that link is less certain.

verses.text: Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone; for your sons are taken away captive, and your daughters into captivity.
verses.arminianNotes: Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone; Arminian readers see the old song of Numbers 21:29 taken up again, now applied to Moab’s sons and daughters going into captivity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Numbers 21:29 has nearly the same words, calling Moab undone, people of Chemosh. The ancient lament from Israel’s wilderness era becomes a present reality.

verses.text: “Yet I will reverse the captivity of Moab in the latter days,” says the LORD. Thus far is the judgment of Moab.
verses.arminianNotes: Yet I will reverse the captivity of Moab in the latter days, Arminian readers see mercy beyond judgment, the LORD’s compassion reaching even to a nation that opposed his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s later mercy toward Moab, shared ground in both traditions. Similar promises are given to Egypt, Ammon, and Elam (46:26; 49:6; 49:39), and Ruth the Moabite is remembered in David’s line (Ruth 4:17).
